questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the law relating to the age of criminal responsibility in achieving justice for young people.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of the law on the age of criminal responsibility; explains the conclusive presumption and doli incapax accurately; integrates relevant legislation, cases, international standards and reform debate
Makes a sound judgement with relevant legal support
Describes the age of criminal responsibility and doli incapax, with some judgement
Provides general information about young offenders or the age of responsibility

required_elements: The conclusive presumption for children under 10
Doli incapax for children aged 10 to 13 and the test in RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53
The international standard in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and its committee's recommended minimum age
Practical limits of doli incapax (arrest, remand and court before it is tested)
The law reform debate (raising the age, alternative responses) and an explicit judgement
questions.model:
The law on the age of criminal responsibility tries to balance the protection of children, whose capacity for moral judgement is still developing, against the community's interest in responding to harmful behaviour. In NSW it achieves this balance only partially, and whether it achieves justice is the subject of significant reform debate.

Under the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) there is a conclusive presumption that a child under 10 cannot commit an offence. For children aged 10 to 13, the common law presumption of doli incapax applies: the child is presumed incapable of criminal responsibility unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew the act was seriously wrong. In RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53 the High Court made clear that this requires proof that the child understood the conduct was seriously wrong in a moral sense, as distinct from merely naughty or mischievous, and that the presumption must be rebutted by evidence about the particular child. This is an important safeguard, because it prevents a child being convicted simply because they did the act.

However, doli incapax has practical limits. It is tested at trial, so a child aged 10 to 13 can still be arrested, held on remand and brought before a court before the presumption is considered. Evidence used to rebut it may also draw on the child's family circumstances and disadvantage, which raises fairness concerns.

International standards provide a benchmark. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) requires states to set a minimum age below which children are presumed not to have the capacity to infringe the criminal law, and to deal with children without resorting to judicial proceedings wherever appropriate. Its monitoring committee has recommended a minimum age of at least 14. Measured against that standard, a minimum age of 10 is low.

Law reform has been debated across Australia, with some jurisdictions raising or committing to raise the minimum age and others choosing not to. Supporters of raising the age argue that early contact with the criminal justice system can entrench offending and that welfare, health and education responses are better suited to young children. Opponents argue that a higher age could leave serious harmful conduct without an adequate response, and that doli incapax already protects children who lack understanding.

Overall, the law is only partly effective in achieving justice for young people. Doli incapax, as clarified in RP v The Queen, is a real safeguard, but the low minimum age sits below the international benchmark and exposes young children to the criminal process. Raising the age, combined with well-resourced alternative responses to harmful behaviour, would better reflect the Convention's emphasis on dealing with children outside the courts wherever appropriate.

questions.model: Crimes against the international community are the most serious crimes of concern to humanity as a whole, such as genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. They are recognised in international law and can be prosecuted by the International Criminal Court under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), as well as by national courts. Transnational crimes, by contrast, are offences that cross national borders, such as drug trafficking, people smuggling, human trafficking and cybercrime. questions.text: Assess the impact of state sovereignty on the effectiveness of measures to deal with international crime.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the impact of state sovereignty on dealing with international crime; explains how sovereignty both limits and enables international and domestic measures; supports the argument with relevant treaties, legislation and cases
Explains the role of state sovereignty, with some judgement and examples
Provides general statements about sovereignty or international crime

required_elements: A definition of state sovereignty
Limits: treaty-based jurisdiction of the ICC, non-party states, reliance on state cooperation for arrests
Complementarity gives states primary responsibility
Domestic measures as exercises of sovereignty (legislation, extradition)
An explicit judgement about the overall impact
questions.model:
State sovereignty is the principle that each state has supreme authority over its territory and people and cannot be bound by international law without its consent. It has a significant, mostly limiting, impact on the effectiveness of measures to deal with international crime, although it also places primary responsibility on states to act.

The International Criminal Court shows the limiting effect most clearly. The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998) is a treaty, so it binds only the states that become parties, and the Court's jurisdiction generally depends on the crime occurring on a state party's territory or being committed by a national of a state party, unless the Security Council refers a situation. Several powerful states are not parties. The Court also has no police force: it relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects, so where a state refuses to cooperate, arrest warrants can remain unenforced for years.

Sovereignty is also built into the Court's design through complementarity: a case is inadmissible where a state is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it. This respects sovereignty while encouraging states to prosecute international crimes themselves.

Domestic measures show the enabling side of sovereignty. Australia has used its law-making power to enact the International Criminal Court Act 2002 (Cth), allowing it to cooperate with the Court, and to include genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, as well as transnational offences such as people trafficking, in the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth). For transnational crime, cooperation depends on arrangements between states, and the Extradition Act 1988 (Cth) allows extradition to be refused on specified grounds, reflecting each state's control over its own legal processes.

Overall, state sovereignty substantially limits the effectiveness of international measures, because they depend on state consent and cooperation. However, where states choose to use their sovereignty to legislate and cooperate, domestic measures can be highly effective.

questions.text: Describe the development of formal statements of human rights after the Second World War.

criteria.descriptor: Provides a detailed and accurate description of the development of formal statements of human rights, with relevant international instruments in sequence

questions.model:
Before the Second World War, human rights were largely a matter for each state's domestic law. The atrocities of the war led states to treat human rights as a matter of international concern. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) included among the purposes of the United Nations promoting and encouraging respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), adopted by the UN General Assembly, was the first comprehensive international statement of rights, covering civil and political rights as well as economic, social and cultural rights. As a declaration it was not binding, so the United Nations then developed binding treaties. In 1966 the General Assembly adopted the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966). Together with the Declaration, these are known as the International Bill of Rights.

Later treaties developed rights for particular groups or issues, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979), the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (1984) and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989). Each is monitored by a committee of independent experts, showing a shift from statements of principle towards mechanisms for monitoring compliance.

questions.model: Treaty law consists of written agreements between states, such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), which bind only the states that consent to them, usually by signing and ratifying. Customary international law is unwritten: it develops when states consistently follow a practice because they believe they are legally obliged to do so, and it can bind states that have not ratified a relevant treaty. The two sources often overlap. For example, the prohibition of torture appears in the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (1984), but it is also widely regarded as part of customary international law, so it binds states whether or not they are parties to that treaty.

questions.text: Explain how Australian courts protect human rights in the absence of a national bill of rights.

criteria.descriptor: Explains clearly how courts protect human rights through the Constitution, the common law and statutory interpretation, with relevant cases, and identifies limits
Explains how courts protect human rights, with relevant examples
Describes some ways courts protect rights
Outlines one way courts protect rights

required_elements: Express constitutional rights enforced by the High Court
Implied constitutional rights: Lange (political communication) and Roach (voting)
Common law protection: Mabo (No 2) and Dietrich
Statutory interpretation and its limits (Momcilovic)
Limits: Parliament can override common law rights; courts act only on cases brought
questions.model:
Australia has no national bill of rights, so the courts protect human rights mainly through the Constitution, the common law and the interpretation of statutes.

First, the High Court enforces the few express rights in the Australian Constitution, such as trial by jury for indictable Commonwealth offences (s 80), freedom of religion from Commonwealth laws (s 116) and acquisition of property on just terms (s 51(xxxi)). It has also found rights implied by the Constitution's structure. In Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation (1997) 189 CLR 520 the Court confirmed an implied freedom of political communication, and in Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007) 233 CLR 162 it held invalid a law that removed the vote from all prisoners serving full-time sentences. These decisions limit what governments can do.

Second, the common law protects rights. In Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 the High Court recognised native title, and in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 it held that a serious criminal trial may be stayed where an accused cannot obtain representation through no fault of their own, protecting the right to a fair trial.

Third, courts interpret legislation consistently with rights where possible, and statutory human rights Acts in Victoria, the ACT and Queensland require this. However, Momcilovic v The Queen (2011) 245 CLR 1 shows the limit: interpretation cannot rewrite a law. Because Parliament can override common law rights by clear words, and courts act only when a case is brought, judicial protection of rights in Australia is real but limited.

questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights; analyses strengths and limitations of UN bodies and mechanisms; supports the argument with relevant treaties, bodies and examples
Makes a sound judgement with relevant examples
Describes UN bodies, with limited judgement

required_elements: Standard-setting: the Charter, the Declaration and the binding covenants
Monitoring: treaty committees and the Universal Periodic Review
Individual complaints: the First Optional Protocol, Toonen and Australia's response
Limits: state sovereignty, non-binding views, Security Council veto
An explicit judgement distinguishing promotion from enforcement
questions.model:
The United Nations is highly effective in promoting human rights, by setting standards and monitoring states, but much less effective in enforcing them, because its mechanisms depend on the consent and cooperation of sovereign states.

The UN's greatest achievement is standard-setting. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) made the promotion of human rights one of the organisation's purposes, and the UN then developed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and binding treaties such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966). These instruments give governments, courts, NGOs and individuals a shared benchmark for judging state conduct.

The UN also monitors compliance. Treaty committees review periodic reports from states parties, and the United Nations Human Rights Council conducts the Universal Periodic Review, in which every UN member state's record is examined by other states. These processes expose shortcomings and produce recommendations, but they rely on peer pressure: a state can ignore recommendations without legal consequence, and the Council's decisions can be shaped by political alliances.

Individual complaints show both the potential and the limits of enforcement. Under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), individuals can complain to the Human Rights Committee. In Toonen v Australia (UN Human Rights Committee, 1994) the Committee found that Tasmanian laws criminalising consensual sex between adult men breached the right to privacy, and the Commonwealth responded with the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 (Cth). Yet the Committee's views are not binding, and compliance depends on the political will of the state concerned.

Coercive action through the Security Council is possible only where violations threaten international peace and security, and any permanent member can veto it, so responses to serious violations are often slow or blocked.

Overall, the UN is effective as a promoter of human rights and as a forum for diplomatic and moral pressure, but its enforcement role is limited by state sovereignty. Its effectiveness ultimately depends on states turning international standards into domestic law, as Australia did after Toonen.

questions.model:
State sovereignty, the principle that each state has supreme authority over its own territory, creates a clear tension with human rights in the treatment of asylum seekers. States have a sovereign right to decide who enters their territory, but they have also accepted international obligations towards people fleeing persecution.

Australia is a party to the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (1951), which defines a refugee and obliges states not to return refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened (non-refoulement). However, the Convention leaves states to decide how they process claims. Australia has exercised its sovereignty through the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), which requires the detention of unlawful non-citizens. Critics, including UN bodies and NGOs, argue that mandatory detention conflicts with the right to liberty, while governments justify it as necessary for border control and security.

The courts show how this tension is managed domestically. In Al-Kateb v Godwin (2004) 219 CLR 562 a majority of the High Court upheld detention that might continue indefinitely. In NZYQ v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (2023) the High Court overruled Al-Kateb, holding that detention cannot validly continue where there is no real prospect of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future. Domestic constitutional limits, rather than international law, have therefore provided the most effective check on sovereign power in this issue.

The tension remains: international standards set expectations, but because they cannot be enforced against a sovereign state, the protection of asylum seekers depends on domestic courts and political will.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain whether the elements of a criminal offence could be established against Jake.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the shove outside the cafe
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Late one night, Jake (aged 24) argues with Chris outside a cafe. Witnesses say Chris swung a punch at Jake, who stepped back and then shoved Chris hard in the chest with both hands. Chris fell backwards, hit his head on the kerb and was taken to hospital with a fractured skull. He has since recovered.

Jake tells police: 'I just wanted him to back off. He'd already thrown a punch and I thought he was going to hit me again. I never meant for him to get hurt like that.'

Jake has been charged with a serious assault offence under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW).

criteria.descriptor: Applies the elements of crime (actus reus, mens rea, causation) and the burden and standard of proof accurately to the scenario, and explains the relevance of self-defence
Explains the elements of crime with clear reference to the scenario
Describes the elements of crime with some reference to the scenario
Outlines actus reus and/or mens rea
Provides some relevant information

required_elements: Burden and standard of proof on the prosecution
Actus reus: the voluntary shove and the resulting injury
Causation: the shove as a substantial and operating cause of the fracture
Mens rea: intention or recklessness, using Jake's statement
Self-defence: belief that the conduct was necessary and a reasonable response; the prosecution must disprove it
questions.model:
To convict Jake, the prosecution must prove each element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt; Jake does not have to prove his innocence, as Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462 established.

The actus reus is the physical element. Jake's voluntary act of shoving Chris in the chest is an application of force, and the prosecution would rely on the witnesses who saw it. It must also prove causation: that the shove was a substantial and operating cause of Chris's fractured skull. Although the injury happened when Chris hit the kerb, the fall was a direct result of the shove, so causation would probably be established.

The mens rea is the mental element. Jake's statement that he 'just wanted him to back off' suggests he intended to push Chris, but not to cause serious injury. Whether the mental element is proved depends on what the particular offence under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) requires, such as intention or recklessness as to a certain kind of harm, so his claim that he 'never meant' the injury is relevant but not necessarily decisive.

The key issue is self-defence. Chris had already thrown a punch, and Jake says he feared another blow. In NSW a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. Once there is evidence of self-defence, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Jake was not acting in self-defence. Stepping back and pushing, rather than striking, may be seen as a reasonable response to a punch, which would make a conviction difficult.

Overall, the actus reus and causation are likely to be proved, but self-defence creates a real doubt about whether Jake is criminally responsible.

Rights after arrest: delayed access to a lawyer; length of detention and questioning
The discretion to exclude improperly or illegally obtained evidence (the drug and the admission)
A judgement about lawfulness and the likely outcome; a possible complaint
questions.model:
The police conduct in this scenario was unlawful in several respects, and this creates a real risk that the key evidence against Lily will be excluded.

First, the search was probably unlawful. Under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), police may search a person without a warrant only if they suspect on reasonable grounds that the person has something such as a prohibited drug. Reasonable suspicion must rest on facts or circumstances, not a hunch. Officer Grant had no information about Lily and acted on 'just a feeling', so the requirement was not met. She also failed to give her name, place of duty and the reason for the search, safeguards that the Act generally requires so that people know who is exercising power over them and why.

Second, Lily's treatment after arrest raises further concerns. A detained person has the right to communicate with a lawyer, and police should not put that off simply to obtain an interview. The Act also limits how long a person may be detained for investigation before being charged or released, unless a detention warrant extends the period. Several hours of questioning without a break, after Lily's request for a lawyer was refused, suggests the safeguards were not respected and that the admission may not have been freely made.

These breaches matter at trial. Under the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW), a court may exclude evidence obtained improperly or in contravention of the law unless the desirability of admitting it outweighs the undesirability of admitting evidence obtained in that way. The court would weigh the seriousness of the breaches, and whether they were deliberate, against the importance of the evidence and the gravity of the offence. Because the offence involves a small quantity of a drug and the breaches were serious, there is a strong argument for excluding both the drug and the admission. Recording the interview helps prove what was said, but it does not cure the earlier unlawfulness.

Overall, the police did not exercise their powers lawfully or fairly. Lily could also complain about the officer's conduct to the NSW Police Force or the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission.

questions.text: Using the hypothetical data in the table, analyse how access to legal representation may affect the fairness of criminal trials.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical data: legal representation in a fictional District Court
stimulus.body:
The figures below are invented for practice. They do not describe any real court and must not be quoted as real statistics.

| Accused's representation (fictional court, one year) | Trials | Acquitted on all charges | Average trial length (days) | Appeals lodged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Private lawyer | 120 | 42 | 6 | 18 |
| Legal aid lawyer | 300 | 84 | 5 | 30 |
| Self-represented | 30 | 3 | 9 | 9 |

Note (also invented): in this fictional court, self-represented accused were mostly charged with less serious indictable offences.

criteria.descriptor: Analyses the hypothetical data accurately to draw sound conclusions about legal representation and fairness; links the data to relevant legal principles and cases; recognises the limits of the data
Describes patterns in the data and links them to legal representation, with some legal support
Refers to the data or to legal representation in general terms

required_elements: Accurate use of the table (acquittals, trial length, appeals) without adding figures
Why representation matters in the adversary system
A link to Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 and the role of legal aid
The data shows an association, not proof of cause; other factors such as the seriousness of charges
A judgement about the effect on fairness
questions.model:
The hypothetical data suggests that access to legal representation has a significant effect on the outcome and efficiency of trials, although the figures alone cannot prove that representation is the cause.

The clearest pattern is in acquittals. About one in three trials with a private lawyer, and just over one in four with a legal aid lawyer, ended in acquittal on all charges, compared with only one in ten for self-represented accused. This is striking because, according to the note, self-represented accused in this fictional court mostly faced less serious charges, which might be expected to favour them. It suggests that unrepresented accused struggle in the adversary system, in which each side must present its own case, test the other side's evidence through cross-examination and make legal submissions. Without legal knowledge, an accused may not recognise inadmissible evidence or available defences.

The data also suggests effects on efficiency. Trials of self-represented accused took the longest on average and produced the most appeals relative to the number of trials. Unrepresented accused may need more explanation from the judge, and errors at trial can lead to appeals, adding cost and delay for everyone, including victims and witnesses.

The comparison between private and legal aid lawyers is less clear. The acquittal figures differ, but the gap is much smaller than the gap with self-represented accused, and it could reflect differences in the types of cases rather than in the quality of representation. Legal aid lawyers appeared in most of the trials, which highlights how much the system depends on public funding.

These patterns support the principle in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 that a trial for a serious offence may be unfair if the accused cannot obtain representation through no fault of their own. However, Dietrich does not create a right to publicly funded counsel, so access to representation depends heavily on legal aid funding. Overall, the data indicates that representation is closely linked to fairness, but a real-world conclusion would need actual, verified statistics that account for the seriousness of the charges and the strength of the evidence.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain the factors a court would consider in sentencing Ben.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the case of Ben
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Ben (aged 22) has pleaded guilty, at the first available opportunity, to a break and enter offence. He broke into a home at night and stole electronic goods. The occupants, an elderly couple, woke to find him in their hallway. As he ran out, Ben pushed the husband aside; the husband fell but was not seriously hurt. A statement from the couple describes ongoing fear and difficulty sleeping.

Ben has two prior convictions for theft. He grew up in a household affected by violence and alcohol abuse and left school at 15. Since his arrest he has completed a residential drug rehabilitation program and has been offered a job. He has written a letter of apology to the couple.

criteria.descriptor: Explains clearly and accurately how aggravating and mitigating factors, the purposes of sentencing and relevant sentencing principles apply to the scenario
Explains some relevant factors with reference to the scenario
Identifies some factors or makes general statements about sentencing

required_elements: Aggravating features from the scenario (vulnerable victims in their home, force used, harm to the victims, prior record)
Mitigating features (early guilty plea, remorse, rehabilitation, deprived background and Bugmy)
Purposes of sentencing that pull in different directions
Method and limits: instinctive synthesis and proportionality
The role of the victims' account of harm
questions.model:
The court would weigh the circumstances of the offence and of Ben himself against the purposes of sentencing in the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW), which include punishment, deterrence, protection of the community, rehabilitation, accountability, denunciation and recognising the harm done to the victims.

Several features make the offence more serious. Breaking into a home at night while the occupants were present is a grave invasion of their security, and the victims were elderly, which the Act recognises as a form of vulnerability that aggravates an offence. Ben also used some force when he pushed the husband aside. The couple's statement describing ongoing fear helps the court understand the harm done. Ben's prior convictions for theft are relevant too: they cannot justify a heavier sentence than the offence deserves, but they reduce the leniency he might otherwise receive and point to a need for specific deterrence.

Other features favour leniency. Ben pleaded guilty at the first available opportunity, which spares the victims from giving evidence and usually entitles him to a reduced sentence. His letter of apology may show remorse. His completion of a residential rehabilitation program and his job offer suggest good prospects of rehabilitation. His upbringing in a household affected by violence and alcohol abuse is relevant under Bugmy v The Queen (2013) 249 CLR 571, where the High Court held that evidence of profound childhood deprivation may be taken into account and does not lose its relevance with time.

The purposes of sentencing pull in different directions. Denunciation and general deterrence call for a firm response to a home invasion, while rehabilitation supports a sentence that does not undo Ben's progress. The judge would not add and subtract fixed amounts for each factor but would weigh them together through instinctive synthesis, as endorsed in Markarian v The Queen (2005) 228 CLR 357, and the final sentence must remain proportionate to the gravity of the offence, as required by Veen v The Queen (No 2) (1988) 164 CLR 465.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical data in the table, evaluate the effectiveness of diversionary options compared with court proceedings for young offenders.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical data: outcomes for young people in a fictional state
stimulus.body:
The figures below are invented for practice. They describe a fictional state, not NSW or any real place, and must not be quoted as real statistics.

| Pathway (young people aged 10 to 17, fictional state, one year) | Young people | Proceeded against again within 12 months | Average days from offence to finalisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Police warning or caution | 4 000 | 800 | 20 |
| Youth justice conference | 1 000 | 250 | 90 |
| Court proceedings | 3 000 | 1 500 | 200 |

Note (also invented): in this fictional state, Aboriginal young people made up a larger share of the court pathway than of the warning and caution pathway.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of diversion compared with court proceedings; uses the hypothetical data accurately and critically, recognising its limits; integrates relevant legislation and international standards
Makes a sound judgement using the data and relevant law
Describes diversion and refers to the data, with limited judgement
Provides general information about young offenders or diversion

required_elements: Accurate use of the table (further proceedings within 12 months; time to finalisation)
The diversion scheme in the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW): warnings, cautions, conferences; an admission is required
Limits of the data: lower-risk young people are more likely to be diverted, so the data cannot prove cause
The equity concern raised by the note (unequal access to diversion)
The international standard in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and an explicit judgement
questions.model:
The hypothetical data suggests that diversion is more effective than court proceedings in reducing further offending and dealing with young people quickly, but the data has important limits, and its note raises a serious question about whether diversion is applied fairly.

In NSW, the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) creates a hierarchy of diversionary options: warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences, which deal with eligible young people outside the court system, usually after they admit the offence. Conferences bring together the young person, their family, the victim and others to agree on an outcome plan, reflecting restorative justice.

The table is consistent with the aims of this scheme. About one in five young people given a warning or caution, and one in four who attended a conference, were proceeded against again within 12 months, compared with half of those dealt with by a court. Diversion was also much faster: warnings and cautions were finalised in an average of 20 days and conferences in 90, compared with 200 days for court matters. Speed matters for young people, because a long period awaiting court can disrupt schooling and family life, and a prompt response is more likely to be understood as a consequence of the behaviour.

However, the data cannot show that diversion caused the lower rate of further offending. Young people who are diverted are often first-time or less serious offenders, while those sent to court may already have a history of offending, so the groups are not comparable. A sound evaluation would compare similar young people who took different pathways.

The note raises a fairness concern. If Aboriginal young people are less likely to receive warnings and cautions, they are more exposed to the court system, its delays and its risk of detention. This would undermine equality before the law, whatever the overall benefits of diversion.

International standards support diversion. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) encourages states to deal with children without resorting to judicial proceedings wherever appropriate and requires detention to be a last resort. Diversion is consistent with these standards because it limits young people's contact with the formal justice system.

Overall, the data suggests diversion is an effective and efficient response for many young offenders, but its effectiveness can only be judged properly with comparable groups, and it achieves justice only if access to it is fair for all young people.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain how the International Criminal Court could deal with the alleged crimes, and the limits it would face.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the conflict in Veldoria
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. Veldoria and Marenta are fictional states.

During a civil war in Veldoria, a rebel commander, Colonel Arak, is accused of ordering attacks on villages in which civilians were deliberately killed, and of recruiting children aged 12 and 13 into his forces. Veldoria has ratified the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998). Its courts have stopped functioning in the areas affected by the war, and no national investigation has begun.

Colonel Arak has fled to neighbouring Marenta, which is not a party to the Rome Statute and has said it will not hand him over to any international court.
evidence_titles: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

criteria.descriptor: Explains accurately how the ICC's jurisdiction, ways of starting a case and admissibility rules apply to the scenario, and the practical and legal limits it faces, with reference to relevant law
Explains some ways the ICC could act, with some reference to the scenario and its limits
Provides general information about the ICC

required_elements: Crimes within jurisdiction: war crimes (attacks on civilians; using children under 15), possibly crimes against humanity
Jurisdiction based on the crimes occurring on a state party's territory; how a case can start
Admissibility: complementarity is satisfied because Veldoria is unable to act and has not acted
Limits: reliance on state cooperation for arrest; Marenta is not a party; the accused must be present at trial
A relevant example, such as the Lubanga case
questions.model:
The International Criminal Court could have jurisdiction over Colonel Arak, but its ability to bring him to trial would depend on cooperation that is unlikely to be given.

The alleged conduct falls within the Court's subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998). Deliberately attacking civilians is a war crime, and if the attacks were part of a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population they could also be crimes against humanity. Recruiting children under 15 into armed forces or groups is also a war crime. In Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012) the Court convicted a militia leader of enlisting and conscripting children under 15, so this charge has a clear precedent.

The Court would have jurisdiction because the crimes were committed on the territory of Veldoria, a state party; it does not matter that Arak has since left. A case could begin through a referral by Veldoria, by the Prosecutor acting on their own initiative with the approval of the Court's judges, or by a Security Council referral.

The case would also be admissible. Under the principle of complementarity, the Court acts only where states are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute. Veldoria's courts are not functioning in the affected areas and no national investigation has begun, so the Court would not be displacing a genuine national process.

The main limit is enforcement. The Court has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects. Marenta is not a party to the Rome Statute and has refused to cooperate, so it has no treaty obligation to hand Arak over unless the Security Council imposes one. Because an accused must be present for trial, an arrest warrant could remain unenforced for years. The Court's response would therefore depend on diplomatic pressure, on Arak travelling to a state willing to arrest him, or on other states prosecuting him under their own laws.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical draft charter in the stimulus, explain how it reflects different types of human rights.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: a draft charter of rights for the fictional Republic of Talmar
stimulus.body:
This draft is invented for practice. Talmar is a fictional state.

Article 1. Every person has the right to vote in free elections and to stand for public office.

Article 2. Every person has the right to free primary and secondary education.

Article 3. The Indigenous peoples of Talmar have the right to determine their own political status and to pursue their economic, social and cultural development.

Article 4. Every person has the right to a healthy environment.

Article 5. The rights in Articles 2 and 4 are to be achieved progressively, as the resources of the Republic allow.

criteria.descriptor: Explains accurately how the draft charter reflects civil and political rights, economic, social and cultural rights, and collective rights, linking each to international instruments and explaining progressive realisation
Explains several types of rights in the draft, with relevant links
Describes some types of rights in the draft
Identifies one or two types of rights
Provides some relevant information

required_elements: Article 1 as a civil and political right
Article 2 as an economic, social and cultural right, and progressive realisation in Article 5
Article 3 as the collective right of self-determination
Article 4 as an emerging environmental right
Why the types differ (individual or collective; immediate or progressive)
questions.model:
The draft charter reflects the main types of human rights recognised in international law, and the differences in how it treats them mirror the international instruments.

Article 1 protects civil and political rights: the right to vote and to stand for office. These individual rights protect a person's participation in government and are set out in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966). They are generally expected to be respected immediately.

Article 2 protects an economic, social and cultural right, the right to education, which appears in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966). Article 5 makes this right subject to progressive realisation 'as the resources of the Republic allow', which mirrors that Covenant's approach: states must take steps, to the maximum of their available resources, towards fully realising these rights, recognising that they often require significant public spending.

Article 3 is a collective right. Self-determination belongs to peoples rather than individuals and appears in Article 1 of both covenants. Its application to Indigenous peoples is recognised in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which is influential but not a binding treaty.

Article 4 reflects an emerging right to a healthy environment. It is collective in nature, because environmental harm affects whole communities and future generations, and it is not set out in the core UN human rights treaties, which shows how the recognition of rights continues to develop. Including it in Article 5 also treats it as a right to be achieved over time.

The draft therefore shows that rights differ in who holds them and in how quickly states are expected to achieve them.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, assess the effectiveness of the domestic legal mechanisms available to Ana.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: Ana's job application
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Ana, who lives in Sydney, applies for an office job with a large private company. At the interview she mentions that she is pregnant. The interviewer tells her the company 'needs someone who will be around for the long haul', and she is not offered the job, although the company had told her she was the best-qualified candidate.

Ana cannot afford a lawyer. She wants the decision reconsidered and an apology, but she is worried that a public dispute will harm her chances of finding other work.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of the domestic mechanisms available to Ana; applies relevant legislation and institutions accurately to the scenario; considers accessibility, cost, remedies and limits
Describes relevant mechanisms with some reference to the scenario and some judgement
Provides general information about discrimination law or human rights

required_elements: Pregnancy discrimination in employment is unlawful under federal and NSW law
A complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission: free, informal, confidential conciliation
If conciliation fails: court proceedings, with cost and publicity concerns
The alternative NSW avenue under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
A judgement about effectiveness for Ana (accessibility against the limits of an individual complaints model)
questions.model:
The domestic mechanisms available to Ana are reasonably effective for her particular needs, because they are accessible and confidential, but they are limited by their reliance on individual complaints and voluntary settlement.

The company's conduct appears to be unlawful. The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) makes discrimination on the ground of pregnancy unlawful in employment, including in deciding who is offered a job. The Act implements Australia's obligations under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979), so Ana's situation shows an international standard being enforced through domestic law.

Ana's first step would be a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission, established by the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth). This mechanism suits her well. It is free and does not require a lawyer, which matters because she cannot afford one. The Commission investigates and tries to resolve complaints through conciliation, a confidential process that avoids the publicity she fears, and outcomes can include an apology, compensation or a change to the employer's practices.

The mechanism also has limits. Conciliation depends on the company's willingness to settle, and the Commission cannot make a binding decision. If conciliation fails, Ana would have to take the matter to court, where proceedings are public, slower and more expensive, and where she might risk paying costs. The system also places the burden on the individual: it responds to Ana's complaint but does little on its own to change the attitudes behind the decision.

Ana could instead use the state system under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW), which also covers pregnancy discrimination and offers a free complaints process, with the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal available if the complaint is not resolved.

Overall, these mechanisms are effective in giving Ana an accessible, low-cost and private avenue, but less effective if the company refuses to cooperate, because the final remedy then depends on costly and public litigation.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses to the use of child soldiers.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: child soldiers in the fictional state of Korvan
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. Korvan is a fictional state.

An armed opposition group in Korvan's northern provinces has recruited several hundred children, some as young as 11, to serve as fighters, messengers and guards. Korvan is a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000) and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998).

An international NGO has published interviews with former child soldiers, and the story has been covered widely by international media. A UN agency is running a program to help released children return to school and their families. Korvan's government says it cannot reach the northern provinces to arrest the group's leaders.

Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

Makes a sound judgement with relevant legal and non-legal examples
Describes legal and/or non-legal responses with some reference to the scenario
Provides general information about child soldiers or human rights

International criminal law: the war crime of using children under 15; complementarity; the Lubanga case
Enforcement limits: the state cannot reach the area; the ICC relies on arrests by states

questions.model:
Legal responses to child soldiers in Korvan set clear standards and allow leaders to be held individually responsible, but they are only partly effective because enforcement depends on control that Korvan does not have. Non-legal responses fill important gaps, particularly in recovery, but cannot stop recruitment on their own.

The treaty framework is strong on paper. As a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), Korvan must take feasible measures to ensure that children under 15 do not take a direct part in hostilities. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000) goes further, providing that armed groups distinct from a state's armed forces should not recruit or use people under 18 in hostilities, and requiring states to take measures to prevent this. The opposition group is clearly in breach of these standards. However, these treaties bind states, and Korvan cannot enforce them in provinces it does not control.

International criminal law targets individuals. Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), enlisting or conscripting children under 15, or using them to participate actively in hostilities, is a war crime. Because the crimes occurred in Korvan, a state party, and Korvan is unable to arrest or prosecute the leaders, the case would be admissible under the principle of complementarity. Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012) shows that such prosecutions can succeed. Yet the Court relies on states to arrest suspects, so while the leaders remain beyond Korvan's reach, an arrest warrant may achieve little except to restrict their travel. In addition, the war crime covers only children under 15, so the recruitment of 15 to 17-year-olds depends on the weaker treaty standard.

Non-legal responses are effective in different ways. The NGO's interviews document abuses, raise awareness and may later provide evidence for prosecutors. Media coverage can build international pressure on the group and on states that support it. The UN agency's program addresses a need the law cannot meet: helping children recover, return to school and reunite with their families. These responses, however, depend on funding and access, and they cannot compel the group to stop.

Overall, the responses are partly effective. The law establishes that recruiting children is unlawful and that leaders can be prosecuted, while non-legal measures support victims and keep the issue visible. Their combined effectiveness will ultimately depend on Korvan regaining control of the north or on the leaders being arrested.

questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the criminal investigation process in balancing the rights of suspects with the protection of the community.

criteria.descriptor: sophisticated, sustained judgement about the effectiveness of the criminal investigation process in balancing suspects' rights and community protection; extensive, accurate knowledge of police powers, rights of suspects, evidence-gathering and bail; integrates relevant legislation, cases, law reform and contemporary evidence; cohesive, logical response using precise legal terminology

sound judgement about the effectiveness of the criminal investigation process; thorough knowledge and understanding of the relevant law; supports the argument with relevant legislation, cases and contemporary evidence; well-organised response using appropriate legal terminology

some judgement about the effectiveness of the criminal investigation process; describes relevant law with some analysis; uses some examples of legislation, cases or other evidence; organised response with some legal terminology
describes aspects of the criminal investigation process; limited or general use of legal examples; limited judgement
makes general or limited statements about the criminal investigation process

required_elements: An explicit, sustained judgement about effectiveness, with criteria (rights, community protection, efficiency)
Police powers of arrest and search and their conditions and safeguards
Detention and interrogation: investigation period, access to a lawyer, the right to silence and its limited exception
Technology and evidence-gathering regulated by warrants and consent (forensic procedures, surveillance)
Exclusion of improperly obtained evidence as an after-the-event safeguard
Bail and remand: the unacceptable-risk test, show cause, and tension with the presumption of innocence
Law reform: at least one reform evaluated for its effect on the balance
questions.model:
The criminal investigation process in NSW is largely effective in balancing the rights of suspects with the protection of the community. Most police powers depend on reasonable suspicion, are subject to procedural safeguards and, for the most intrusive powers, require independent judicial authorisation. However, the balance is fragile. Many safeguards depend on police discretion and on remedies that apply only after a breach has occurred, and several reforms, particularly to bail and the right to silence, have shifted the balance towards community protection at some cost to the presumption of innocence. This response evaluates effectiveness by asking whether the process protects the community efficiently while respecting suspects' rights to liberty, privacy and a fair trial.

The foundation of the balance is the presumption of innocence. In Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462 the House of Lords described the prosecution's duty to prove guilt as the 'golden thread' of the criminal law, and that principle is applied in Australia. A suspect under investigation has not been convicted of anything, so police powers that restrict liberty or privacy must be justified by the needs of the investigation, not by an assumption of guilt.

Police powers of arrest and search largely reflect this principle. The Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) consolidates most police powers and attaches conditions to them. A police officer may arrest without a warrant only if the officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the person has committed an offence and is satisfied that arrest is reasonably necessary for a listed reason, such as preventing the person from fleeing or protecting evidence. This necessity requirement encourages police to use less intrusive options, such as a court attendance notice, which is an effective protection of liberty. When exercising powers, police must generally give their name, place of duty and the reason for the exercise of the power, so that people can understand and challenge what is happening to them. These conditions are effective in principle. In practice, however, reasonable suspicion is a flexible standard that is applied first by individual officers on the street, so the protection depends heavily on police training, culture and oversight, including complaints to the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission. The law sets a sound balance, but its effectiveness varies with how discretion is exercised.

Detention and interrogation show a similar pattern. After arrest, the Act allows a person to be detained for investigation only for a limited investigation period, which can be extended only by a detention warrant, and detained people have rights such as communicating with a lawyer or a relative. Extra protections apply to vulnerable people, including children. The right to silence is protected by the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW), which generally prevents an unfavourable inference being drawn from a suspect's silence during official questioning. Parliament has, however, created a limited exception for some serious indictable offences, where a special caution has been given and a lawyer is present. This reform was justified as a way of stopping suspects from 'ambushing' the prosecution with a defence raised for the first time at trial, but critics argue it erodes a fundamental protection. Because the exception is narrow and depends on legal advice being available, it has a limited practical effect, so the right to silence remains a largely effective safeguard.

Technology has strengthened the community-protection side of the balance while creating new risks to privacy. DNA evidence can identify offenders, link crimes and exclude innocent suspects. The Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 (NSW) regulates when forensic samples may be taken from suspects, offenders and volunteers, requiring consent or an order in many cases, and when DNA profiles must be destroyed. Covert surveillance is even more intrusive, so the Surveillance Devices Act 2007 (NSW) generally requires a warrant for police to use listening, optical, tracking or data surveillance devices. Requiring an independent judicial officer to authorise these powers is one of the most effective features of the process, because it tests the justification for intrusion before it occurs. Its limitation is that warrant applications are made without the suspect being heard, so the quality of the scrutiny depends on the issuing officer.

When safeguards are breached, the main remedy comes at trial. The Evidence Act 1995 (NSW) gives a court a discretion to exclude evidence obtained improperly or in contravention of the law unless the desirability of admitting it outweighs the undesirability of admitting evidence obtained in that way. This is a balanced approach: automatic exclusion could let guilty people go free because of minor errors, while automatic admission would reward unlawful conduct. Its weakness is that it protects only suspects who are prosecuted and who contest the evidence; a person who is unlawfully searched and released without charge has no comparable remedy at trial.

Bail and remand are where the balance has shifted most clearly towards community protection. The Bail Act 2013 (NSW) requires a bail authority to refuse bail only if there is an unacceptable risk, for example that the accused will fail to appear, commit a serious offence or endanger the safety of victims or the community, which is a rational, risk-based test. However, amendments added 'show cause' requirements for certain serious offences, under which the accused must show why their detention is not justified. Those amendments were made in response to public concern about particular bail decisions, and the Act has been amended a number of times since. Requiring an unconvicted person to justify their liberty sits uneasily with the presumption of innocence, and people held on remand may lose employment, housing and family contact even if they are later acquitted or receive a non-custodial sentence. Frequent, reactive amendment also makes the law less stable and harder to apply consistently. The bail system therefore protects the community, but at a real cost to the rights of some accused people.

Overall, the criminal investigation process is effective to a considerable extent. The legal framework in the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), together with judicial authorisation of intrusive powers and the courts' discretion to exclude improperly obtained evidence, sets a sound balance between investigating crime and protecting suspects. That balance is weakened, however, by its dependence on police discretion and by reforms that have tended to favour community protection, particularly in bail. The process would be more effective if reforms were based on evidence about their effects rather than on reaction to individual cases, and if oversight of everyday police powers were as strong as the judicial control of the most intrusive ones.

questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of sentencing and punishment in achieving justice for offenders, victims and society.

criteria.descriptor: sophisticated, sustained judgement about the effectiveness of sentencing and punishment in achieving justice for offenders, victims and society; extensive, accurate knowledge of sentencing purposes, factors, discretion, penalties and post-sentencing; integrates relevant legislation, cases, law reform, reports and inquiries; cohesive, logical response using precise legal terminology

sound judgement about the effectiveness of sentencing and punishment; thorough knowledge and understanding of the relevant law; supports the argument with relevant legislation, cases and contemporary evidence; well-organised response using appropriate legal terminology

makes general or limited statements about sentencing and punishment

required_elements: An explicit, sustained judgement covering offenders, victims and society
Statutory purposes of sentencing and aggravating and mitigating factors
Judicial discretion and its limits: instinctive synthesis, proportionality, standard non-parole periods
The role of victims in sentencing
Types of penalties and alternatives (community-based orders, restorative approaches)
Post-sentencing considerations such as parole
Over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and relevant reports or inquiries

questions.model:
Sentencing and punishment in NSW achieve justice for offenders, victims and society to a considerable extent, mainly because judicial discretion allows sentences to be individualised within a framework of statutory purposes and principles set by Parliament and the High Court. They are less effective, however, in reducing reoffending and in addressing the over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in custody. The system is therefore better at punishing fairly than at preventing future offending, and justice for society depends on more than the sentence itself.

The statutory framework sets out what sentencing is meant to achieve. The Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) lists the purposes of sentencing: adequate punishment, deterrence of the offender and others, protection of the community, rehabilitation, accountability, denunciation of the conduct, and recognition of the harm done to the victim and the community. It also lists aggravating and mitigating factors that the court must take into account. Listing multiple purposes is a strength, because it recognises that justice has several dimensions. Yet the purposes often conflict: a long sentence may serve denunciation and deterrence while undermining rehabilitation. The framework therefore leaves the crucial balancing to the judge.

Judicial discretion is the main reason sentencing achieves justice for offenders. In Markarian v The Queen (2005) 228 CLR 357 the High Court endorsed 'instinctive synthesis', under which the judge weighs all relevant factors together to reach a single sentence rather than adding and subtracting fixed amounts. This allows the court to respond to the circumstances of each case. In Bugmy v The Queen (2013) 249 CLR 571 the High Court held that evidence of profound deprivation in an offender's upbringing may be taken into account and does not lose its relevance over time, although the Court required the offender's own circumstances to be established rather than assumed from membership of a group. Discretion is also limited by principle: Veen v The Queen (No 2) (1988) 164 CLR 465 established that a sentence must not exceed what is proportionate to the gravity of the offence merely to protect society. These principles make sentencing fair to offenders, because like cases are treated alike in principle and no offender is punished more than the offence deserves.

The cost of discretion is perceived inconsistency, which affects justice for society. Similar offences can attract different sentences, and public criticism that sentences are too lenient has led Parliament to structure discretion. Standard non-parole periods are one example. In Muldrock v The Queen (2011) 244 CLR 120, however, the High Court held that a standard non-parole period is only one guidepost and not a mandatory starting point. This shows the ongoing tension between Parliament's wish for consistency and the courts' commitment to individualised justice. On balance the courts' approach better serves justice, because rigid sentencing rules can produce disproportionate punishment in unusual cases, and appeals by both the offender and the prosecution provide a mechanism for correcting inconsistent sentences.

Victims have gained a stronger place in sentencing, although their role is deliberately limited. The sentencing framework allows victims to describe the harm they have suffered, and recognising that harm is one of the statutory purposes of sentencing. This acknowledges victims as participants rather than mere witnesses. However, the sentence is not determined by the victim's wishes, because that would make outcomes depend on the attitudes of individual victims rather than on the seriousness of the offence. The system is effective in giving victims a voice, but some victims remain dissatisfied with the outcome.

The range of penalties and alternatives also affects whether justice is achieved. NSW courts can impose community-based orders, such as intensive correction orders served in the community, as well as full-time imprisonment. Community-based sentences allow offenders to keep employment and family ties and can address causes of offending, such as drug dependence, which serves rehabilitation and, in the long term, community safety. Restorative approaches, such as circle sentencing for some Aboriginal offenders in the Local Court, involve Elders and the community in the sentencing process. These alternatives show that sentencing can pursue justice for society by reducing future harm, not only by punishing past harm.

Post-sentencing processes extend this balance. The Crimes (Administration of Sentences) Act 1999 (NSW) governs the administration of sentences, including parole decisions by the State Parole Authority. Parole supports rehabilitation by giving offenders a supervised transition back into the community, while allowing the Authority to refuse or revoke parole where the risk to the community is too high. Parole decisions are often controversial after high-profile reoffending, which shows that public confidence depends on how risks are managed after the sentence is imposed.

The greatest limitation of sentencing is its failure to resolve the over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in custody. The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody: National Report (1991) recommended that imprisonment be used only as a last resort. More than two decades later, the Australian Law Reform Commission's Pathways to Justice: Inquiry into the Incarceration Rate of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples (ALRC Report 133) examined why over-representation had continued and made recommendations on matters including sentencing options and justice reinvestment. That the issue had to be examined again shows that sentencing law alone cannot address underlying causes such as disadvantage, and that recommendations are only as effective as their implementation.

Overall, sentencing and punishment are effective in achieving justice for offenders, because discretion guided by principle produces individualised and proportionate sentences, and reasonably effective for victims, who now have a recognised voice. They are less effective for society as a whole, because punishment does not reliably reduce reoffending and has not resolved the over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Further law reform that expands community-based and restorative options, implemented consistently with the Pathways to Justice recommendations, would increase the system's effectiveness.

questions.text: To what extent does the criminal justice system achieve justice for young offenders?

criteria.descriptor: sophisticated, sustained judgement about the extent to which the criminal justice system achieves justice for young offenders; extensive, accurate knowledge of the age of criminal responsibility, rights when questioned, the Children's Court, penalties, diversion and bail; integrates relevant legislation, cases, international standards and law reform; cohesive response using precise legal terminology

sound judgement about the extent to which the criminal justice system achieves justice for young offenders; thorough knowledge and understanding of the relevant law; supports the argument with relevant legislation, cases and contemporary evidence; well-organised response using appropriate legal terminology

some judgement about the extent to which the criminal justice system achieves justice for young offenders; describes relevant law with some analysis; uses some examples of legislation, cases or other evidence; organised response with some legal terminology
describes aspects of the treatment of young offenders; limited or general use of legal examples; limited judgement
makes general or limited statements about the treatment of young offenders

required_elements: An explicit judgement about the extent, sustained throughout
The age of criminal responsibility and doli incapax (RP v The Queen)
The rights of young people when questioned or arrested
The Children's Court, its principles and penalties, and the protection of identity
Diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
Bail and remand of young people, and detention as a last resort
International standards (CRC) and at least one law reform issue
questions.model:
The criminal justice system achieves justice for young offenders to a significant extent. NSW law recognises that young people are less mature and more capable of rehabilitation than adults, and it provides distinct protections, a specialist court and a structured system of diversion. However, the low minimum age of criminal responsibility, the use of remand and the gap between the law's principles and the experience of disadvantaged young people, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people, limit the extent to which justice is achieved. Justice for young offenders is assessed here by whether the system holds young people accountable in a way that is fair, proportionate to their age and likely to reduce future offending.

The starting point is the age of criminal responsibility. Under the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW), a child under 10 cannot be guilty of an offence. Children aged 10 to 13 are protected by the presumption of doli incapax, which the prosecution must rebut by proving beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew the act was seriously wrong. In RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53 the High Court confirmed that this means seriously wrong in a moral sense, not merely naughty, and that the evidence must concern the particular child. Doli incapax is a meaningful safeguard. Its limitation is that it is tested late, so a young child may already have been arrested, remanded and brought to court. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) requires states to set a minimum age, and its monitoring committee has recommended an age of at least 14. Measured against that benchmark, NSW's minimum age of 10 is low, and some Australian jurisdictions have moved to raise their minimum age. This is the area in which the system is least effective.

The law provides stronger protections for young people when they are questioned. Under the framework of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), children are treated as vulnerable people, so a support person who is not a police officer should be present during questioning, and they can contact a lawyer. The Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) reinforces these protections by limiting the use of admissions made by a child without a suitable adult present. These rules are effective in protecting the reliability and fairness of admissions, but their value depends on the quality of the support person, who may be a parent without legal knowledge.

The Children's Court and the principles that govern it are a major strength. The Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) sets out principles that recognise that children bear responsibility for their actions but, because of their immaturity, need guidance and assistance, and that it is desirable for their education or employment to continue without interruption. Proceedings are generally closed to the public, and publishing the name of a child involved in criminal proceedings is generally prohibited, which protects young people from lasting stigma. Penalties range from dismissals and good behaviour bonds to control orders served in detention, and in many cases a conviction is not recorded against a younger child. These features make the system more proportionate and more focused on rehabilitation than the adult system, which is consistent with the requirement in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) that detention be used only as a last resort and for the shortest appropriate time.

Diversion is the system's most effective feature. The Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) creates a hierarchy of warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences, which allow eligible young people who admit an offence to be dealt with outside court. Conferences bring together the young person, their family and the victim to agree on an outcome plan, so they promote accountability and repair harm while avoiding a conviction. Diversion is quicker and less stigmatising than court. Its limits are that it depends on an admission and on the exercise of police discretion, so young people who distrust police or who are unaware of the scheme may miss out, and access may be uneven across communities.

Bail and remand are the system's main weakness. The Bail Act 2013 (NSW) applies to young people, and Parliament has amended it in ways that make bail harder to obtain in some circumstances, including for some young people charged with serious offences while already on bail. Remand interrupts schooling and family life and exposes young people to detention before any finding of guilt, which sits uneasily with the presumption of innocence and with the principle that detention should be a last resort. Young people without stable accommodation can be particularly affected, because suitable bail conditions may be harder to meet.

These weaknesses fall most heavily on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people. The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody: National Report (1991) recommended that imprisonment be used only as a last resort, and that principle is most directly tested in decisions about diversion and bail. Where Aboriginal young people are less likely to receive diversion or bail, the system's protective principles are not being applied equally, which undermines justice regardless of how sound the law appears on paper.

Overall, the criminal justice system achieves justice for young offenders to a significant but incomplete extent. Doli incapax, the protections during questioning, the Children's Court and, above all, diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) reflect a sound understanding of young people's capacity and potential for rehabilitation. The low minimum age of responsibility, the use of remand and unequal access to diversion prevent the system from fully achieving justice. Raising the age of criminal responsibility, reducing the use of remand and ensuring fair access to diversion would bring the system closer to the standards in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989).
