questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of domestic and international measures in dealing with international crime.

criteria.descriptor: sophisticated, sustained judgement about the effectiveness of domestic and international measures in dealing with both crimes against the international community and transnational crimes; extensive, accurate knowledge of the relevant institutions and laws; integrates relevant treaties, legislation, cases and law reform; cohesive response using precise legal terminology

sound judgement about the effectiveness of domestic and international measures in dealing with international crime; thorough knowledge and understanding of the relevant law; supports the argument with relevant legislation, cases and contemporary evidence; well-organised response using appropriate legal terminology

some judgement about the effectiveness of domestic and international measures in dealing with international crime; describes relevant law with some analysis; uses some examples of legislation, cases or other evidence; organised response with some legal terminology
describes aspects of international crime; limited or general use of legal examples; limited judgement
makes general or limited statements about international crime

required_elements: An explicit judgement distinguishing transnational crimes from crimes against the international community
Domestic measures: Commonwealth offences, extradition, police cooperation, with a case example
International measures: the Genocide Convention, ad hoc tribunals and the ICC
Complementarity and domestic implementation of the Rome Statute
Limits: state sovereignty, non-parties, reliance on arrests by states, Security Council politics
An ICC case example and an evaluation of its significance
Law reform in international criminal law
questions.model:
Domestic and international measures are moderately effective in dealing with international crime, but their effectiveness differs between the two categories of crime. Transnational crimes, such as drug trafficking, people trafficking and cybercrime, are dealt with reasonably effectively when states cooperate, because they are prosecuted under domestic laws that can be enforced. Crimes against the international community, such as genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, are dealt with less effectively, because the international institutions that address them depend on the consent and cooperation of sovereign states. Effectiveness is evaluated here by the extent to which these measures hold offenders accountable, deter offending and respect state sovereignty and fair process.

Domestic law is the main response to transnational crime, and in Australia it is reasonably effective. The Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) contains offences for serious drug trafficking, slavery and slavery-like practices, people trafficking and terrorism, allowing Commonwealth prosecutors to deal with crimes that cross borders. R v Tang (2008) 237 CLR 1 shows these laws working. The case involved women brought to Australia to work in a brothel, and the High Court held that slavery includes exercising over a person any of the powers attaching to the right of ownership, even without legal ownership. The decision confirmed that Australia's slavery offences reach modern forms of exploitation, which shows domestic law implementing international obligations effectively. However, domestic prosecutions depend on detection and on cooperation with other states to gather evidence and locate offenders.

Cooperation between states is therefore essential, and it is only partly effective. The Extradition Act 1988 (Cth) allows Australia to surrender people to, and seek them from, other countries, subject to legal requirements and grounds for refusal. Police agencies share intelligence and coordinate operations against drug and trafficking syndicates. These arrangements work well between states with similar legal systems and good relations, but they are slow and can fail where a state lacks an arrangement with Australia, where laws differ, or where offenders operate from states unwilling or unable to act. Cybercrime highlights the problem, because offenders can act anonymously from anywhere in the world. The effectiveness of measures against transnational crime is thus limited less by the law than by state capacity and willingness to cooperate.

For crimes against the international community, the development of international law has been a major achievement. The Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948) defined genocide and obliged states parties to prevent and punish it. In the 1990s the Security Council established ad hoc international criminal tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda, which showed that individuals, including senior leaders, could be prosecuted internationally. The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998) then created a permanent court with jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. Law reform has continued within this framework: after amendments agreed at a review conference in 2010, the Court's jurisdiction over the crime of aggression was activated in 2018. Together these developments established the principle that individuals are criminally responsible for the most serious international crimes, whatever their position.

The International Criminal Court's record shows both its significance and its limits. In Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012), its first trial judgment, the Court convicted a militia leader of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him to 14 years' imprisonment. The case confirmed that the recruitment of child soldiers is a serious international crime and gave practical effect to individual responsibility. However, the proceedings took years, and critics argue that the Court has completed relatively few trials for an institution of its size. Its greatest limitation is enforcement: it has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects. Its jurisdiction generally depends on the crime occurring in a state party or being committed by a national of a state party, unless the Security Council refers a situation, and several major powers are not parties. Security Council referrals are subject to the veto of the permanent members, so political considerations can determine which situations reach the Court.

The principle of complementarity partly addresses these limits by making national courts the first line of response. Under the Rome Statute, a case is inadmissible where a state with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it. Australia has implemented this by enacting the International Criminal Court Act 2002 (Cth), which allows it to cooperate with the Court, and by including genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), so these crimes can be prosecuted in Australian courts. Complementarity respects sovereignty and encourages states to build their own capacity. Its weakness is that the states where these crimes occur are often those least able or willing to prosecute, especially where the alleged offenders hold power.

Overall, domestic and international measures are moderately effective. Against transnational crime, domestic law such as the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), supported by extradition and police cooperation, is reasonably effective where states cooperate. Against crimes against the international community, the Genocide Convention and the Rome Statute have created a strong normative framework and some significant convictions, but enforcement remains limited by state sovereignty, the absence of key states and the politics of the Security Council. The effectiveness of both sets of measures ultimately depends on the willingness of states to cooperate, which is the most important factor in whether international crime is dealt with justly.

questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of international and domestic legal measures in promoting and enforcing human rights.

criteria.descriptor: sophisticated, sustained judgement about the effectiveness of international and domestic legal measures in promoting and enforcing human rights; extensive, accurate knowledge of UN mechanisms, the Australian Constitution, statute law, courts and statutory bills of rights; integrates relevant treaties, legislation, cases and law reform; cohesive response using precise legal terminology

sound judgement about the effectiveness of international and domestic legal measures in promoting and enforcing human rights; thorough knowledge and understanding of the relevant law; supports the argument with relevant legislation, cases and contemporary evidence; well-organised response using appropriate legal terminology

makes general or limited statements about the promotion and enforcement of human rights

required_elements: An explicit judgement distinguishing promotion from enforcement
International measures: the UN Charter, treaties, monitoring, the Human Rights Council and individual complaints
A complaint example and Australia's response (Toonen)
The Australian Constitution: express and implied rights and their limits
Statute law: anti-discrimination Acts, the Australian Human Rights Commission, parliamentary scrutiny
Statutory bills of rights in Victoria, the ACT and Queensland, and their limits
Law reform and an evaluation of the effect of state sovereignty
questions.model:
International and domestic legal measures are effective in promoting human rights, by setting clear standards and creating institutions that monitor and publicise compliance. They are less effective in enforcing human rights. International mechanisms depend on the consent and cooperation of sovereign states, and Australia's domestic system relies on a patchwork of constitutional, statutory and common law protections rather than a national bill of rights. Effectiveness is evaluated here by whether these measures prevent violations, provide remedies to individuals and lead to lasting legal change.

International law has been highly effective in establishing human rights standards. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) made promoting respect for human rights one of the purposes of the United Nations, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) turned many of the rights in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) into binding treaty obligations. These standards give governments, courts, NGOs and individuals a common benchmark against which state conduct can be judged.

International monitoring promotes compliance, but enforcement is weak. Treaty committees review periodic reports from states, and the United Nations Human Rights Council conducts the Universal Periodic Review, under which the human rights record of every UN member state is examined by other states. These processes rely on peer pressure: they can expose violations and produce recommendations, but they cannot compel a state to act, and political alliances can shape the Council's decisions. Where a state is indifferent to criticism, monitoring has little effect.

Individual complaints mechanisms show what international measures can achieve when a state is willing to respond. Under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), individuals in Australia can complain to the UN Human Rights Committee once domestic remedies are exhausted. In Toonen v Australia (UN Human Rights Committee, 1994) the Committee found that Tasmanian laws criminalising consensual sex between adult men breached the right to privacy. The Commonwealth responded by enacting the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 (Cth), and Tasmania repealed the laws in 1997. Toonen is a clear example of a non-binding international finding leading to domestic law reform. However, the Committee's views are not binding, and their effect depends on a government's political willingness to act, so the mechanism is effective only where that will exists.

Domestically, the Australian Constitution provides limited but enforceable protection. It contains only a few express rights, such as trial by jury for indictable Commonwealth offences and freedom of religion from Commonwealth laws, and it can be changed only by referendum. The High Court has found further protections implied by the Constitution's system of government. In Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation (1997) 189 CLR 520 the Court confirmed an implied freedom of political communication, and in Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007) 233 CLR 162 it held invalid a law disqualifying all prisoners serving full-time sentences from voting. Because these protections bind Parliament, they are the strongest form of enforcement in Australian law. Their limitation is scope: the implied freedom is a limit on government power rather than a personal right, and most human rights have no constitutional protection.

Statute law fills many of these gaps. The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) implements Australia's obligations to eliminate racial discrimination, and the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) established the Australian Human Rights Commission, which investigates and conciliates complaints and promotes human rights. These mechanisms are accessible, free and effective in resolving many individual complaints. Yet ordinary statutes can be amended or overridden by later legislation, and the complaints model depends on individuals coming forward. At the law-making stage, the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) requires statements of compatibility for new bills and established the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights. This promotes rights-aware law-making, but Parliament can still pass laws that the Committee considers incompatible with human rights.

Statutory bills of rights in three jurisdictions show an alternative model. The Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT), the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic) and the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) require laws to be interpreted compatibly with human rights where possible, require compatibility statements for bills, and allow the Supreme Court to declare that a law cannot be interpreted compatibly, without affecting its validity. These 'dialogue' models are effective in making rights part of everyday government decision-making while preserving parliamentary sovereignty. Their limits were shown in Momcilovic v The Queen (2011) 245 CLR 1, where the High Court held that the Victorian Charter's interpretation provision operates within the ordinary limits of statutory interpretation and does not allow courts to rewrite legislation. NSW and the Commonwealth have no equivalent law, so protection depends on where a person lives, and whether a national human rights Act should be enacted remains a live law reform debate.

Overall, international and domestic legal measures are effective in promoting human rights and moderately effective in enforcing them. The UN system has set strong standards and, as Toonen shows, can prompt domestic reform, but it cannot compel unwilling states. In Australia, the Constitution, statute law and statutory bills of rights provide real but fragmented protection that Parliament can usually override. The most effective outcomes occur when international standards are implemented in domestic law and enforced by domestic institutions, which suggests that strengthening domestic implementation is the most important reform for improving the enforcement of human rights in Australia.

questions.model:
The development of human rights has led to their effective recognition to a very large extent, but to their effective protection only to a moderate extent. Over several centuries, rights that were once privileges of a narrow class have come to be recognised as belonging to every person, set out in international instruments and accepted by almost every state. However, recognition has consistently run ahead of protection, because many instruments are not binding, some rights are to be achieved only progressively, and enforcement depends on sovereign states. This response assesses the extent to which each stage of development turned recognition into protection.

Early developments established the principle that power is limited by law, but they protected only some people. The Magna Carta (1215) limited the power of the Crown and promised that free men would not be imprisoned or deprived of their rights except by lawful judgment or the law of the land. It is rightly seen as a milestone in the rule of law, yet its protections originally applied to a narrow class. Later developments, such as the abolition of slavery, the gradual extension of the right to vote and the recognition of workers' rights, each extended rights to groups previously excluded. In Australia, for example, women gained the right to vote in federal elections in 1902, but many Aboriginal people were excluded from the federal franchise until 1962. These developments show that recognition has expanded gradually and unevenly, often only after sustained political struggle.

The most significant development came after the Second World War. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) made promoting respect for human rights one of the purposes of the new organisation, so that a state's treatment of its own people became a matter of international concern. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) then set out, for the first time, a comprehensive list of civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights belonging to everyone. As a General Assembly declaration it was not binding, which limited its direct protective effect. That gap was partly closed by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966), which made these rights binding on states that become parties. Recognition became near universal, but protection still depended on each state's ratification and implementation.

The two covenants also reveal different levels of protection for different rights. Civil and political rights are generally expected to be respected immediately, while economic, social and cultural rights, such as health and education, are to be realised progressively to the maximum of a state's available resources. This reflects practical reality, because these rights often require significant public spending, but it means that rights such as an adequate standard of living are recognised long before they are protected in practice, especially in poorer states.

Customary international law has strengthened protection for the most fundamental rights. The prohibition of torture appears in the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (1984), but it is also widely regarded as part of customary international law, so it binds states that have not ratified the treaty. This development is significant because it removes the protection of some rights from the choice of individual states. Yet even customary prohibitions are violated where states face no consequences, which shows that legal status alone does not guarantee protection.

The development of rights for particular groups shows both progress and its limits. The Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979) required states to eliminate discrimination against women in public and private life, and Australia implemented its obligations through the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth), which gives individuals an enforceable complaints process. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) recognised children as holders of rights, including the principle that detention should be a last resort. Collective rights have also developed. The right of peoples to self-determination appears in Article 1 of both covenants, and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) recognised the rights of Indigenous peoples, although Australia voted against it in 2007 before endorsing it in 2009, and it is not a binding treaty. Domestic courts have also contributed: in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 the High Court rejected terra nullius and recognised native title, a landmark recognition of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' rights in Australian law. These developments show recognition being converted into protection where states pass implementing laws or courts give rights legal effect.

Overall, the development of human rights has led to their effective recognition to a very large extent: rights are now understood as universal, are set out in binding treaties and, in some cases, form part of customary law. It has led to their effective protection only to a moderate extent, because many instruments are not binding, economic and social rights are realised progressively, and enforcement depends on state sovereignty. The most effective protection has come where international recognition has been implemented in domestic law, as with the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth), or recognised by domestic courts, as in Mabo. The continuing development of human rights therefore depends less on new statements of rights than on states giving existing rights legal effect.
